Monday. Hafsa took out the sanction letter and read every line. Interest rate. When the grace period ends. First instalment. Charges for paying early. She underlined two words she did not know.

Tuesday. At the bank, Jagdish, the loan officer, explained each word using simple examples. Hafsa asked what happens if a part payment is made and wrote the answer beside the line. Nothing was rushed.

Thursday. On one page Hafsa listed the terms in her own handwriting and pinned it above the desk. Only then did she open a spreadsheet to think about a repayment plan. She felt steadier, knowing she was no longer working from guesses.

qa.a: Jagdish, the loan officer, explained each word using simple examples.

qa.q: How did Hafsa feel after listing the terms on one page?

qa.a: Hafsa could ask for the answers in writing or bring a trusted person to the next visit, because unclear terms should not be guessed.

passage:
Anirban, before you sign anything, sit down. Your Pema aunty took an education loan too, back when I went to Pune for nursing.
Everyone told me what to do. Pay it fast, pay it slow, don't pay anything till you get a job. I was confused, so I did one thing first. I took the sanction letter to the bank and sat at the loan officer's desk with a notebook.
I wrote down four things. The interest rate: ten and a half percent. When the grace period ended: six months after the course. The EMI after that. And whether I'd be charged for paying early. That last one I didn't understand, so I asked the officer to explain it twice, slowly.
Only after that page was full did I decide anything. Now it's your turn, Anirban. Where is your sanction letter?

qa.q: What interest rate did Pema write down?
How did young Pema feel before going to the bank?
qa.a: Confused and a little overwhelmed by everyone's conflicting advice.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Pema's story?
qa.a: Deciding to write down the loan terms before choosing any plan, and asking the officer to explain the early-payment charge until it made sense.

qa.q: How might the loan officer have seen young Pema that day?
qa.a: As a careful borrower who came with a notebook and asked questions, which likely made the conversation easier for the officer too.

grounding: Shows a borrower noting the interest rate, grace period end, EMI and prepayment charges from the sanction letter, and asking the bank to explain, before deciding anything.

passage:
Avni reached the branch at 1:40, twenty minutes before the loan desk shut for lunch, with her sanction letter in a plastic folder and six people ahead of her in the queue.
She used the wait. On the back of the folder she wrote four headings: rate, when the moratorium ends, EMI, charges for paying early. Then she hunted for each one in the letter. Rate: 9.8 percent, floating. Moratorium: ends twelve months after the course. EMI: ₹7,900 after that. Prepayment: one clause she couldn't make sense of.
At 1:58 she reached the desk. The officer, Nandini, glanced at the clock. Avni held up the folder. 'Just one thing. What does this line about part-payment mean?'
Nandini read it and explained: no charge for paying extra on a floating rate. Avni wrote 'NONE' in capitals.
The shutter came down behind her. Only now, with all four boxes filled, would she start thinking about a plan.

qa.q: What is the EMI after the moratorium?
Why did Avni hold up the folder instead of asking about everything?
qa.a: She was anxious about the lunch deadline and focused, wanting the one unclear clause answered before the desk shut.

qa.q: What else could Avni do now that all four boxes are filled?
qa.a: Compare a few repayment choices against these exact terms, and ask a qualified adviser if any choice is still unclear.

qa.q: How might Nandini see Avni's question at 1:58?
qa.a: With lunch approaching, Nandini likely found one clear question easy to answer and appreciated that Avni had done the reading first.

grounding: Shows a borrower listing the rate, moratorium end, EMI and prepayment terms from the sanction letter and asking the bank about the unclear clause before planning.
